title: Dividing by a literal multiplies by its reciprocal
verdict: `x / c` is `x * (1 / c)`: not correctly rounded, NaN or inf for a subnormal `c`; `49.0 % 49.0` is 49.0
description: When one operand of `/`, `//` or `%` on floats has length 1 and the other more (a literal, `pl.lit`, or a one-row column against a longer one), Polars computes the reciprocal of the divisor once and multiplies: `x / c` is `x * (1 / c)`, `x // c` is `floor(x * (1 / c))`, `x % c` is `x - c * floor(x * (1 / c))`. Two roundings replace one, so `x / c` can miss the IEEE quotient by an ulp: `49.0 / 49.0` is 0.9999999999999999, and then `49.0 // 49.0` is 0.0 and `49.0 % 49.0` is 49.0. Recorded as PL-3.

For a subnormal `c` the reciprocal overflows to inf: `0.0 / 1e-310` is NaN where IEEE gives 0.0, and `1e-300 / 1e-310` is inf where IEEE gives 1e10 (`%` gives -inf). The same holds for `Float32` below about 2.9e-39.

On a one-row frame both sides have length 1 and the IEEE kernel runs, so the one-row probes do not show it. Two columns of equal length use `l / r`. Both engines share the kernels, but the streaming engine picks one per morsel: its in-memory source cuts a frame into morsels of `len.div_ceil(k · threads)` rows, so a frame shorter than the thread count streams as one-row morsels and divides exactly, and a frame a little longer mixes both results in one column. With `POLARS_MAX_THREADS=10`, `49.0 / 49.0` on 4 or 10 rows gave 1.0, on 11 rows both 1.0 and 0.9999999999999999, on 40 rows 0.9999999999999999. With one thread a 4-row frame gives 0.9999999999999999, and `% 49.0` gives 49.0. So the result depends on `POLARS_MAX_THREADS` and `POLARS_IDEAL_MORSEL_SIZE`.
polars-scalar-divisor records the same finding from #590's probe and is the id the engine tables cite.

Integer `/` casts both sides to `Float64` and runs the same kernel, so a literal integer divisor takes the reciprocal too: `Int64` `49 / 49` is 0.9999999999999999 and `5 / 3` is 1.6666666666666665 (polars-int-true-divide). A division by an aggregate (`x / x.max()`) has a length-1 divisor as well. `DataFrame / 3` repeats the scalar to the frame's height and divides exactly.
The `truediv` docs and the user guide call float division IEEE 754, which this contradicts: PL-8. No upstream test pins this; it may change between versions.
reference: `divide` on doubles is the IEEE quotient, rounded once (`rounding: TIE_TO_EVEN`), and creates no NaN from non-NaN inputs other than `0/0` and `inf/inf`, which raise. `sverify_fmod` is the truncated remainder, smaller than the divisor in magnitude.

evidence.note: `floor_div`, `trunc_div` and `mod` with a literal divisor use `inv = 1 / rhs`.
`legacy_div_scalar`, which `ChunkedArray / ChunkedArray` reaches for floats, is `true_div_scalar`.
`/` on floats is `left / right` on the columns.
`+ - * // %` on two ChunkedArrays: equal lengths take the array kernel, a length-1 side the scalar kernel.
A literal is a scalar column, passed to the operation as a one-value Series.
The streaming engine evaluates each expression with polars-expr's `PhysicalExpr` on every morsel, so it runs the same kernels.

notes: `impl_float_arith_kernel!` is one macro instantiated for `pf16`, `f32` and `f64`, so `Float32` and `Float64` run the same operations. The streaming engine evaluates expressions through polars-expr on each morsel (`StreamExpr` in crates/polars-stream/src/expression.rs), so it shares these kernels with the in-memory engine. The broadcast in `apply_binary_kernel_broadcast_owned` sends a length-1 right side to the scalar kernel, and a literal reaches it as a one-value Series.
Read at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3). The streaming engine evaluates expressions through polars-expr on each morsel (crates/polars-stream/src/expression.rs), so these kernels serve both engines.

evidence.note: pl.DataFrame({'x': [0.0, 1e-300, 2.0]}).select(pl.col('x') / 1e-310, pl.col('x') % 1e-310, pl.col('x') // 1e-310): [nan, inf, inf], [nan, -inf, -inf], [nan, inf, inf]. On pl.DataFrame({'x': [0.0]}): 0.0.
pl.DataFrame({'x': [0.0, 1.0, 0.5]}, schema={'x': pl.Float32}).select(pl.col('x') / pl.lit(1e-40, dtype=pl.Float32)): [nan, inf, inf].

pl.LazyFrame({'x': [49.0] * 5000 + [0.0]}).select(pl.col('x') / 49.0, pl.col('x') % 49.0).collect(engine='streaming'): 0.9999999999999999 and 49.0 for x = 49.0. The same query on a 4-row LazyFrame gave the IEEE results (1.0, 0.0, and 1e-300 / 1e-310 = 10000000000.00003) under streaming and the deviations under engine='in-memory'.

provenance.notes: Polars 2.1.0, macOS arm64. Streaming splits a small frame into one-row morsels, where both sides have length 1 and the IEEE kernel runs; morsels of two rows or more take the literal path, as the in-memory engine does.

evidence.note: `test_list_arithmetic_values`, `Float32`: 1 // 0 is inf, 1 % 0 NaN, 1 / 0 inf, 0 // 0 NaN, 0 % 0 NaN, 0 / 0 NaN
`test_list_arithmetic_values`, `Float32` (picked so nothing upcasts to `Float64`): 7 // 3 is 2, -5 % 3 is 1, 2 / 128 is 0.015625

notes: The broadcast cases of the test run `x / c`, `x // c` and `x % c` with a one-row `c` against three rows, the reciprocal path, in `Float32`: 1 / 0 is inf, 0 / 0 NaN, 7 // 3 is 2, -5 % 3 is 1. Each of these agrees with the IEEE quotient too, so the test neither confirms nor contradicts PL-3; no Polars test at py-2.1.0 asserts an inexact quotient of a broadcast divisor (searched `py-polars/tests/unit` for float divisions by literals and scalar aggregates). The rows stay at the source.

Polars's CI runs the unit tests by default, where a lazy `collect()` without `engine` runs the streaming engine (also once with `POLARS_IDEAL_MORSEL_SIZE=4`), and again with `POLARS_ENGINE_AFFINITY=in-memory` (.github/workflows/test-python.yml#L55-L78, #L168-L178); eager `Series` and `DataFrame` calls run in memory. Read at tag py-2.1.0 (commit 7f902bd3), not run.

Streaming agrees with memory on 9 000 rows: `49.0 % 49.0` is 49.0, `49.0 // 49.0` 0.0, `0.0 / 1e-310` NaN, `1e-300 / 1e-310` inf. So PL-3 holds on the streaming engine when the morsels hold more than one row.

`python -m sverify_dev.probe_polars --diff --write` runs each observation (`STREAMING_OBSERVATIONS`, python/tools/sverify_dev/probe_polars.py) with `collect(engine='in-memory')` and `collect(engine='streaming')` and records both results. Polars 2.1.0 (Python), macOS arm64.

provenance.notes: polars-scalar-divisor records the same finding from #590's probe and is the id the engine tables cite.

evidence.note: morsel length = len.div_ceil(k * num_pipelines): which kernel runs depends on threads and POLARS_IDEAL_MORSEL_SIZE
integer / integer casts both sides to Float64 first, so a literal integer divisor takes the float reciprocal kernel too

provenance.notes: Corrected the description: it said a small frame under streaming gives the IEEE results; that holds only while the frame is shorter than the thread count (in_memory_source.rs#L118-L122). Added integer `/` and division by an aggregate, which take the reciprocal too.

evidence.sql: POLARS_MAX_THREADS=10 POLARS_IDEAL_MORSEL_SIZE=64: pl.LazyFrame({'x': [49.0] * n}).select(pl.col('x') / 49.0).collect(engine='streaming') for n in (4, 10, 11, 40)

evidence.note: no upstream test pins pl.col(x) / literal on two rows or more; test_df.py#L2982-L3016 checks DataFrame / scalar, which materializes the scalar and runs the column kernel

provenance.notes: From the reverse pass's check of PL-3, which this fact records.
